claims.text: Atomic-size mismatch and suppression of long-range ordering induce local lattice distortions in noble-metal-based HEA nanomaterials.
Tailored local lattice distortions govern reliable formation of noble-metal-based HEA nanomaterials.
Tailored local lattice distortions govern the catalytic performance of noble-metal-based HEA nanomaterials.
Local lattice distortions modify the electronic structure of surface sites.
The distortion-induced electronic structure optimizes the binding energies of key reaction intermediates.
A narrow, optimized annealing window can preserve high lattice strain and short-range order without extensive phase segregation or long-range ordering.
Higher-temperature or prolonged annealing promotes ordering or phase separation.
Local lattice distortions and short-range-order clusters create nonuniform d-band electronic states at surface atomic sites.
Atomic-scale distortions can shift the d-band center of surface noble-metal atoms.
Shifting the local electronic structure tunes adsorption energies for catalytic intermediates.
Tuned adsorption energies reduce the reaction barrier and increase conversion rates.
Retention of a defect-rich, uniform nanostructure ensures reliable material formation.
Optimally annealed samples will exhibit a lower catalytic onset potential than more ordered, phase-segregated controls.
Optimally annealed samples will exhibit higher catalytic current density or turnover frequency than more ordered, phase-segregated controls.
Excessive or prolonged annealing diminishes lattice strain and produces less favorable electronic structures for catalysis.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to noble-metal-based HEA nanomaterials having significant atomic-size disparity.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to particles smaller than approximately 10 nm.
Surface effects and lattice distortions are dominant in the specified sub-10-nm particle-size regime.
Surface segregation of individual elements may independently influence catalytic activity.
